title: Turning Text into Numbers (Classical)
description: The classical toolkit for representing text numerically: bag of words, TF-IDF, n-grams, and putting it all together into a working text classifier.

lessons.title: Bag of Words
lessons.description: Learn the simplest way to turn a document into a vector of numbers a model can actually use.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain how the bag-of-words representation works and describe its key limitation.

sections.title: 👜 The core idea
sections.content:
**Bag of words (BoW)** represents a document as a vector counting how many times each word in a fixed vocabulary appears — completely ignoring word order, hence the "bag" (like dumping all the words into a bag and just counting them).

```python
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer

docs = ["the cat sat on the mat", "the dog sat on the log"]

vectorizer = CountVectorizer()
X = vectorizer.fit_transform(docs)

print(vectorizer.get_feature_names_out())
# ['cat', 'dog', 'log', 'mat', 'on', 'sat', 'the']
print(X.toarray())
# [[1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2],   ← "the cat sat on the mat"
#  [0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 2]]   ← "the dog sat on the log"

sections.title: ✅ Why it's still useful
sections.content: Despite (or partly because of) its simplicity, bag-of-words is fast, easy to compute, and works surprisingly well as a baseline for many text classification tasks — especially when the specific vocabulary used (rather than exact phrasing or grammar) is the main useful signal, like distinguishing spam from legitimate email based on which words tend to appear.

sections.title: 😕 The obvious limitation: word order is thrown away
sections.content: "The dog bit the man" and "the man bit the dog" produce the *exact same* bag-of-words vector — every word appears the same number of times, just in a different order that BoW completely discards. Any meaning that depends on word order or sentence structure is invisible to this representation.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Using bag-of-words for tasks where word order or grammar genuinely matters.** For translation, generation, or nuanced language understanding, throwing away order loses too much information.

**Not accounting for vocabulary size on large corpora.** A large collection of documents can produce an enormous vocabulary, leading to very high-dimensional (and often sparse) vectors — this is manageable but worth being aware of.

**Assuming bag-of-words captures meaning the way a human would.** It's purely a word-count representation — it has no notion of synonyms, context, or semantic similarity between words.

questions.question: What does a bag-of-words vector represent?
options: The exact sequence of words in a document, preserving order
How many times each word in a fixed vocabulary appears in a document, ignoring order
A summary of the document's grammar
The sentiment score of a document
questions.explanation: Bag of words counts word occurrences per document, completely discarding the order those words appeared in — hence treating the document like an unordered 'bag' of words.

questions.question: Why do 'the dog bit the man' and 'the man bit the dog' produce identical bag-of-words vectors?
options: They actually don't produce identical vectors
Bag of words only counts word frequency and completely ignores the order words appear in, so both sentences have the same word counts
Bag of words automatically detects and corrects for meaning
The two sentences use different words
questions.explanation: Since bag of words is purely a count of how many times each vocabulary word appears, and both sentences use exactly the same words the same number of times, their BoW vectors are identical — despite having very different meanings.

questions.question: For what kind of task does bag of words tend to work reasonably well as a baseline?
options: Tasks that depend heavily on exact word order, like translation
Tasks where the presence of specific vocabulary words is the main useful signal, like spam detection
Generating grammatically correct new sentences
Understanding sarcasm and tone
questions.explanation: When the key signal is simply which words tend to show up (rather than their order or grammatical role), bag of words can be a fast, effective baseline — spam detection is a classic example, since certain words are strongly associated with spam regardless of their position.

questions.question: In the bag-of-words example from the lesson, what feature values would 'the' have across two documents that both contain it twice?
options: It would always be 0
It would be counted as 2 in each document that contains it twice
Bag of words ignores the word 'the' automatically
It can only be represented as a fraction
questions.explanation: Bag of words simply counts occurrences — a word appearing twice in a document gets a count of 2 in that document's vector, as shown in the lesson's example.

questions.question: What is the dimensionality of a bag-of-words vector typically based on?
options: The number of sentences in a single document
The size of the fixed vocabulary across the document collection
The number of documents only
The length of the shortest document
questions.explanation: Each dimension in a bag-of-words vector corresponds to one word in the vocabulary, so the vector's length matches the vocabulary size.

questions.question: Why is 'the cat sat on the mat' and 'the dog sat on the log' example used in the lesson?
options: To show that bag of words cannot process more than one document
To illustrate how each document is converted to a numeric vector counting word occurrences
To demonstrate that bag of words can capture word order
To show that bag of words removes all common words automatically
questions.explanation: The example concretely shows how CountVectorizer transforms each document into a vector of word counts against the shared vocabulary.

questions.question: What is a practical benefit of bag of words despite its simplicity?
options: It always outperforms every other text representation
It's fast, easy to compute, and works well as a baseline for many text classification tasks
It requires no computation at all
It automatically understands synonyms
questions.explanation: Despite ignoring word order and meaning, bag of words remains a fast and surprisingly effective baseline, especially for vocabulary-driven tasks like spam detection.

questions.question: What information about a document does bag of words completely discard?
options: The total word count
The order in which words appear
Which specific words appear at all
The vocabulary size
questions.explanation: By treating a document as an unordered collection of word counts, bag of words throws away all information about the sequence or order in which words originally appeared.

lessons.title: TF-IDF: Weighting Words by How Distinctive They Are
lessons.description: Learn a smarter version of word counting that downweights common words and highlights distinctive ones.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain what TF-IDF measures and why it often outperforms plain word counts.

sections.title: ❓ The problem with raw counts
sections.content: In plain bag-of-words, a word like "the" gets a huge count in every document, while a genuinely distinctive, topic-relevant word (like "mitochondria" in a biology article) might appear just once or twice. Raw counts alone don't reflect how *informative* a word actually is for distinguishing one document from another.

sections.title: 📊 Term Frequency × Inverse Document Frequency
sections.content:
**TF-IDF** combines two ideas into one score for each word in each document:

• **Term Frequency (TF)** — how often the word appears in *this* document (like a plain count, often normalized)
• **Inverse Document Frequency (IDF)** — how *rare* the word is across the *entire collection* of documents — common words across many documents get a low IDF, rare words get a high IDF

```
TF-IDF(word, document) = TF(word, document) × IDF(word)
```

A word that appears often in one document but rarely across the whole collection gets a high TF-IDF score — exactly the kind of distinctive, informative word you'd want to weight heavily.

sections.title: 🛠️ Using TF-IDF in practice
sections.content:
```python
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer

docs = ["the cat sat on the mat", "the dog sat on the log"]

vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer()
X = vectorizer.fit_transform(docs)

print(vectorizer.get_feature_names_out())
print(X.toarray())
# words like "the" (appearing in both documents) get a low weight
# words like "cat"/"dog" (distinctive to one document) get a higher weight
```

TF-IDF remains a strong, fast, interpretable baseline for tasks like document search, information retrieval, and text classification — often outperforming plain bag-of-words counts.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming TF-IDF understands meaning.** It's still fundamentally a word-counting technique — it just weights those counts more cleverly. It has no concept of synonyms or semantic similarity (that's what embeddings, covered next module, are for).

**Forgetting IDF is computed from the whole document collection, not a single document.** A word's IDF score depends on how it's distributed across your *entire* corpus — the same word can have very different IDF scores in different collections.

**Applying TF-IDF and expecting it to handle word order.** Like plain bag-of-words, TF-IDF still ignores the order words appear in within a document.

questions.question: What does the IDF (inverse document frequency) part of TF-IDF measure?
options: How many times a word appears in one specific document
How rare a word is across the entire collection of documents — common words get a low value, rare words get a high value
The total number of documents in the collection
The grammatical category of a word
questions.explanation: IDF specifically captures rarity across the whole document collection — a word appearing in almost every document gets a low IDF (since it's not distinctive), while a word appearing in only a few documents gets a high IDF.

questions.question: Why does TF-IDF typically outperform plain word counts (bag of words) for many tasks?
options: It processes documents faster in every case
It downweights common, uninformative words and upweights rarer, more distinctive words, better reflecting which words actually carry useful signal
It captures word order, unlike bag of words
It requires no vocabulary at all
questions.explanation: By combining how often a word appears in a document with how rare it is across the whole collection, TF-IDF highlights genuinely distinctive words rather than just the most frequent ones, which raw counts alone can't do.

questions.question: What limitation does TF-IDF share with plain bag-of-words?
options: Neither approach can be computed for large document collections
Both ignore the order in which words appear within a document
Both require labeled training data
Neither can be used for text classification
questions.explanation: TF-IDF is still fundamentally a word-count-based representation — like plain bag of words, it discards the sequence/order of words within a document, so it can't capture meaning that depends on word order.

questions.question: What problem with raw word counts does TF-IDF address?
options: Raw counts take too long to compute
Raw counts don't reflect how informative a word is, since very common words like 'the' get inflated counts regardless of topical relevance
Raw counts can never be represented as numbers
TF-IDF actually has no advantage over raw counts
questions.explanation: Plain counts overweight extremely frequent but uninformative words, while TF-IDF's IDF component specifically downweights words that are common across the whole corpus.

questions.question: What does Term Frequency (TF) measure in TF-IDF?
options: How rare a word is across the whole corpus
How often a word appears within a specific document
The grammatical category of the word
The total number of documents in the corpus
questions.explanation: TF captures how frequently a specific word appears within a single document, forming one half of the overall TF-IDF score.

questions.question: Would a word appearing in every single document in a corpus tend to get a high or low IDF score?
options: A very high IDF score
A very low IDF score, since it isn't distinctive
IDF cannot be computed for such a word
IDF only applies to rare words
questions.explanation: IDF is designed to give common, non-distinctive words (that appear in nearly every document) a low score, since they don't help distinguish one document from another.

questions.question: For what kinds of applications does the lesson say TF-IDF remains a strong choice?
options: Only for generating new creative text
Document search, information retrieval, and text classification
Only for image classification tasks
Exclusively for speech recognition
questions.explanation: The lesson highlights document search, information retrieval, and text classification as tasks where TF-IDF remains a strong, fast, and interpretable baseline.

questions.question: Does TF-IDF have any built-in concept of word meaning or synonyms?
options: Yes, it fully understands semantic relationships between words
No, it's still fundamentally a word-counting technique with no concept of synonyms
TF-IDF only works with synonyms, not exact word matches
TF-IDF eliminates the need for a vocabulary
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly warns that TF-IDF is still a word-counting technique — it weights counts more cleverly but has no built-in notion of semantic similarity, which is what embeddings later address.

lessons.title: N-grams: Capturing a Little Bit of Word Order
lessons.description: Learn a simple trick that lets count-based methods capture some local context, without a full sequence model.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain what n-grams are and describe the tradeoff involved in choosing n.

sections.title: 🔗 The core idea
sections.content:
An **n-gram** is a contiguous sequence of `n` tokens. Instead of treating each word as an independent unit, n-grams treat short sequences of consecutive words as single units — recovering a small amount of local word-order information that plain bag-of-words completely throws away.

```python
text = "the cat sat on the mat"

# unigrams (n=1): individual words
# ["the", "cat", "sat", "on", "the", "mat"]

# bigrams (n=2): pairs of consecutive words
# ["the cat", "cat sat", "sat on", "on the", "the mat"]

# trigrams (n=3): triples of consecutive words
# ["the cat sat", "cat sat on", "sat on the", "on the mat"]
```

sections.title: 🎯 Why this small change helps
sections.content:
Bigrams and trigrams can capture short but meaningful phrases that unigrams alone would miss — "not good" as a bigram is a very different (and more informative) signal than seeing "not" and "good" as two unrelated, independent tokens.

```python
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer

vectorizer = CountVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2))  # unigrams AND bigrams together
X = vectorizer.fit_transform(["the movie was not good"])
print(vectorizer.get_feature_names_out())
# includes both "not" and "not good" as separate features
```

sections.title: ⚖️ The tradeoff: vocabulary size explodes
sections.content: Every increase in `n` multiplies the number of possible combinations, dramatically growing the vocabulary size — most of those n-grams appearing only once or twice in the data (a **sparsity** problem). In practice, unigrams plus bigrams (occasionally trigrams) is a common sweet spot; going much higher rarely pays off and can hurt more than help, especially with limited data.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming higher n is always better.** Very high-order n-grams create an enormous, extremely sparse vocabulary that's hard to learn useful patterns from, especially with a modest dataset.

**Forgetting n-grams still only capture *local*, short-range context.** A bigram or trigram can't capture a relationship between words far apart in a sentence — for that, you eventually need the sequence models or attention mechanisms covered in Deep Learning and NLP's later modules.

**Not considering the added computational cost.** More n-gram features mean a larger vocabulary and more computation — worth weighing against the actual benefit for your specific task.

questions.question: What does a bigram represent?
options: A single word
A pair of two consecutive words treated as one unit
The entire document as one unit
A random sample of words from the document
questions.explanation: A bigram (n=2) groups two consecutive tokens together as a single feature, capturing a small amount of local word-order information that individual word counts (unigrams) would miss on their own.

questions.question: Why might including bigrams help a sentiment classifier that plain unigrams alone would miss?
options: Bigrams are always faster to compute than unigrams
A phrase like 'not good' as a bigram captures meaning that treating 'not' and 'good' as separate, independent words would lose
Unigrams can't be used for sentiment analysis at all
Bigrams eliminate the need for any vocabulary
questions.explanation: As independent unigrams, 'not' and 'good' don't convey that they're negating each other — capturing 'not good' as a single bigram preserves that locally important relationship between adjacent words.

questions.question: What's the main tradeoff of using higher-order n-grams (like n=4 or n=5)?
options: They always improve model accuracy with no downside
The vocabulary size grows dramatically and most n-grams appear rarely, creating a sparse, harder-to-learn-from feature space
Higher-order n-grams are only usable for numeric data
They eliminate the need for tokenization
questions.explanation: As n increases, the number of distinct possible n-grams grows quickly, and most specific ones appear only rarely in real data — this sparsity generally outweighs the benefit beyond unigrams and bigrams (occasionally trigrams) for most practical tasks.

questions.question: What does a trigram represent?
options: A single isolated word
A sequence of three consecutive tokens treated as one unit
The entire document treated as one token
Two unrelated words picked at random
questions.explanation: A trigram (n=3) groups three consecutive tokens together, capturing slightly more local context than a bigram or unigram alone.

questions.question: According to the lesson, what is a common practical sweet spot for n-gram range in real applications?
options: Only very high-order n-grams like n=10
Unigrams plus bigrams, occasionally trigrams
Character-level n-grams exclusively
n-grams are never combined with unigrams
questions.explanation: The lesson notes that unigrams plus bigrams (sometimes trigrams) is a common practical sweet spot, since going much higher rarely pays off and can hurt more than help.

questions.question: What happens to vocabulary size as n increases in n-gram modeling?
options: It stays exactly constant
It grows dramatically, with most n-grams appearing only once or twice (a sparsity problem)
It always shrinks
Vocabulary size is unrelated to n
questions.explanation: Larger n multiplies the number of possible token combinations, causing vocabulary size to explode and most specific n-grams to appear only rarely in the data.

questions.question: Can n-grams capture long-range relationships between words far apart in a sentence?
options: Yes, n-grams capture relationships across an entire document
No — n-grams only capture local, short-range context
N-grams eliminate the need for any other sequence modeling technique
N-grams can only be used for single-word sentences
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly notes that n-grams only capture local, short-range context — for longer-range dependencies, sequence models or attention mechanisms are needed instead.

questions.question: In the sklearn example using ngram_range=(1, 2), what does the vectorizer produce?
options: Only bigram features, no unigrams
Both unigram and bigram features together, like 'not' and 'not good' as separate features
Only trigram features
No features at all
questions.explanation: Setting ngram_range=(1, 2) tells CountVectorizer to include both single-word (unigram) and two-word (bigram) features in the resulting vocabulary.

lessons.title: Text Classification with Classical Methods
lessons.description: Put bag-of-words, TF-IDF, and classical ML together to build a working text classifier.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can describe the end-to-end pipeline for building a classical text classifier.

sections.title: 🧩 Putting the pieces together
sections.content:
A classical text classification pipeline combines everything from this module and the machine learning course:

1. **Preprocess** the text (tokenize, optionally remove stop words, stem/lemmatize)
2. **Vectorize** it into numbers (bag-of-words or TF-IDF, optionally with n-grams)
3. **Train** a classical ML classifier (logistic regression and Naive Bayes are especially popular choices for text) on the resulting vectors
4. **Evaluate** using the same metrics from the machine learning course (accuracy, precision/recall, F1 — matched to what actually matters for the task)

sections.title: 🛠️ A conceptual pipeline
sections.content:
```python
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline

pipeline = Pipeline([
    ("tfidf", TfidfVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2), stop_words="english")),
    ("classifier", LogisticRegression()),
])

pipeline.fit(X_train_texts, y_train_labels)
predictions = pipeline.predict(X_test_texts)
```

Wrapping preprocessing and modeling into a single pipeline (as shown here) also helps avoid data leakage — the vectorizer is fit only on training data, exactly as covered in the data science course.

sections.title: ✅ Why this classical approach still matters
sections.content: Even in an era of large language models, this classical pipeline remains genuinely useful: it's fast, cheap to train, easy to interpret (you can literally inspect which words drive a prediction), and a strong baseline that's often surprisingly hard to beat for straightforward tasks like spam detection or basic topic classification — especially with limited data or tight computational budgets.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Fitting the vectorizer on the full dataset before splitting into train/test.** Just like scaling or encoding in the data science course, this leaks test-set vocabulary statistics into training — fit the vectorizer on training data only.

**Jumping straight to a complex deep learning model without trying this baseline first.** A classical pipeline is fast to build and often reveals whether a much more expensive approach is actually going to be worth it.

**Ignoring class imbalance in text classification.** Just like in the ML course, if one class (like "not spam") vastly outnumbers another, accuracy alone can be misleading — the same precision/recall guidance from the ML course applies directly here.

questions.question: What are the typical stages of a classical text classification pipeline?
options: Train a model directly on raw text strings with no preprocessing
Preprocess the text, vectorize it into numbers, train a classical ML model, then evaluate it
Only vectorization is needed — no model training required
Skip preprocessing and go straight to deep learning
questions.explanation: A classical pipeline combines text preprocessing (tokenizing, optionally stemming/removing stop words), numerical vectorization (like TF-IDF), classical model training, and evaluation — bringing together techniques from both this course and the machine learning course.

questions.question: Why should a TF-IDF vectorizer be fit only on the training data, not the full dataset?
options: Fitting on the full dataset is computationally impossible
Fitting on the full dataset leaks vocabulary and frequency statistics from the test set into training, similar to the data leakage covered in the data science course
TF-IDF vectorizers can only be fit once per project
There's no real issue either way
questions.explanation: This mirrors the exact same data leakage concern from the data science course — fitting any preprocessing step (including a TF-IDF vectorizer) on the full dataset lets test-set information influence training in a way that makes evaluation dishonest.

questions.question: Why does a classical text classification pipeline remain useful even with modern large language models available?
options: It always achieves higher accuracy than any other approach
It's fast, cheap to train, highly interpretable, and often a strong, hard-to-beat baseline for straightforward tasks with limited data or compute
Large language models cannot process text at all
Classical approaches are required by law for text classification
questions.explanation: Despite being simpler, classical pipelines remain genuinely practical — fast to train, easy to interpret, and often surprisingly competitive for tasks like spam detection, especially when data or computational resources are limited.

questions.question: What is the first stage of a classical text classification pipeline?
options: Training the classifier directly on raw, unprocessed text
Preprocessing the text, such as tokenizing and optionally removing stop words or stemming/lemmatizing
Evaluating the model's accuracy
Deploying the trained model
questions.explanation: The pipeline begins with preprocessing steps like tokenization and optional normalization, before the text is vectorized and used to train a model.

questions.question: Which classical models are mentioned as especially popular choices for text classification?
options: K-means and PCA
Logistic regression and Naive Bayes
GANs and autoencoders
Convolutional neural networks only
questions.explanation: The lesson specifically calls out logistic regression and Naive Bayes as especially popular classical model choices for text classification tasks.

questions.question: What is a benefit of wrapping preprocessing and modeling into a single sklearn Pipeline object?
options: It makes the code run on a different programming language
It helps avoid data leakage by fitting the vectorizer only on training data
It automatically improves accuracy to 100%
It eliminates the need for any evaluation step
questions.explanation: Using a Pipeline ensures the vectorizer is fit only on the training data during cross-validation or train/test splits, preventing test-set information from leaking into training.

questions.question: Why does the lesson recommend being cautious about class imbalance in text classification?
options: Class imbalance never occurs in text data
If one class vastly outnumbers another, accuracy alone can be misleading, just as in the ML course
Imbalanced classes always improve model performance
Precision and recall don't apply to text classification
questions.explanation: Just as in the machine learning course, a highly imbalanced class distribution (like far more 'not spam' than 'spam' examples) can make plain accuracy a misleading metric — precision and recall give a more honest picture.

questions.question: Why does a classical text classification pipeline remain useful even in an era of large language models?
options: It's always more accurate than any large language model
It's fast, cheap to train, interpretable, and a strong baseline especially with limited data or compute
Large language models cannot process text data at all
Classical pipelines require no data to train
questions.explanation: The lesson highlights that classical pipelines remain genuinely practical for straightforward tasks, offering speed, interpretability, and strong baseline performance without the cost of large language models.
